text: On the half decayed veranda. <break time="0.8s" /> Of a small wooden house. <break time="0.8s" /> Near the edge of a ravine. <break time="0.8s" /> Outside Winesburg, Ohio. <break time="0.8s" /> A fat little old man. <break time="0.8s" /> Walked nervously up and down. <break time="0.8s" /> Beyond a long field. <break time="0.8s" /> Where clover had been planted. <break time="0.8s" /> But only yellow mustard weeds had grown. <break time="0.8s" /> He could see the highway. <break time="0.8s" /> And a wagon full of berry pickers. <break time="0.8s" /> Coming home. <break time="0.8s" /> The young men and women in the wagon. <break time="0.8s" /> Laughed and shouted noisily. <break time="0.8s" /> And a girls voice called to him. <break time="0.8s" /> Oh, you Wing Biddlebaum, comb your hair. <break time="0.8s" /> The man was bald. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet his nervous little hands. <break time="0.8s" /> Fluttered about his bare white forehead. <break time="0.8s" /> As though he were arranging. <break time="0.8s" /> A mass of tangled hair. <break time="0.8s" /> Wing Biddlebaum had lived. <break time="0.8s" /> In Winesburg for twenty years. <break time="0.8s" /> But he did not think of himself. <break time="0.8s" /> As a part of the life of the town. <break time="0.8s" /> He was always frightened and troubled. <break time="0.8s" /> By a ghostly crowd of doubts. <break time="0.8s" /> And among all the people of Winesburg. <break time="0.8s" /> Only one had ever come close to him. <break time="0.8s" /> That one was George Willard. <break time="0.8s" /> A young reporter on the town newspaper, the Winesburg Eagle. <break time="0.8s" /> With whom Wing had formed. <break time="0.8s" /> Something like a friendship. <break time="0.8s" /> Now, as the sun went down. <break time="0.8s" /> The old man walked up and down the veranda. <break time="0.8s" /> Hoping that George would come. <break time="0.8s" /> And spend the evening with him.
